<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
The category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{ELHSLat}}\) is arithmetical, and therefore satisfies \(n\)-normality of Higgins commutators. It also satisfies transitivity of normality, algebraic cartesian closedness, and the condition {\rm (SSH)}{}. However, \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{ELHSLat}}\) does not satisfy normality of unions, nor is it action accessible. \hfill \qed
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{BouJa Charact}
	A variety is semi-abelian if and only if the corresponding algebraic theory contains exactly one constant \(0\) and for some natural number \(n\) we have
	\begin{itemize}
		\item \(n\) binary operations \(\alpha_i\) such that \(\alpha_i(x,x) =0\) for all \(i=1, \dots , n\),
		\item an \((n+1)\)-ary operation \(\Theta\) such that \(\Theta(\alpha_1(x,y), \dots , \alpha_n(x,y),y)= x\).\hfill \qed
	\end{itemize}
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
A non-empty subset \(K\) of a Heyting semilattice \(H\) is a \textbf{filter} of~\(H\) when:
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item if \(k, k' \in K\), then \(k \wedge k' \in K\);
		\item if \(k \in K\) and \(h \in H\) with \(h \geqslant k\), then \(h \in K\).
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{Lemma Normal is Filter}
	A non-empty subset \(K\) of a Heyting semilattice \(H\) is the kernel of some morphism \(f \colon H \to H'\) of Heyting semilattices if and only if \(K\) is a filter. In categorical terminology, filters correspond to \textbf{normal subobjects} in the category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{HSLat}}\). \hfill \qed
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{example non semi-boolean}
	Let \(H\) be the Heyting semilattice with Hasse diagram
	\[
		\xymatrix@!=0ex{
		& 1 &\\
		& z\ar@{-}[u] &\\
		x\ar@{-}[ur] & & y \ar@{-}[ul]\\
		& 0\ar@{-}[ul]\ar@{-}[ur] &
		}
	\]
	Then the pseudo-join \(\curlyvee\) is not the join, since \(x \curlyvee y = 1\).
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{proposition equivalences semi-boolean}
	For a Heyting semilattice \(H\), the following conditions are equivalent:
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item \(H\) is semi-Boolean;
		\item \(x \curlyvee (y \curlyvee z) = (x \curlyvee y) \curlyvee z\);
		\item \(x \leqslant y\) implies \((z \curlyvee x) \leqslant (z \curlyvee y)\);
		\item \(\curlyvee\) distributes over \(\wedge\);
		\item \(\wedge\) distributes over \(\curlyvee\);
		\item \((x \curlyvee y) \shortrightarrow z = (x \shortrightarrow z) \wedge (y \shortrightarrow z)\).\hfill \qed
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
Any linearly ordered set with a top element can be endowed with a semi-Boolean Heyting semilattice structure. Indeed, given a linearly ordered set \(S\) with top element \(1\), the meet of two elements is their minimum and the join is their maximum. The implication is defined by
	\[
		x \shortrightarrow y =
		\begin{cases}
			1 & \text{if } x \leqslant y, \\
			y & \text{otherwise},
		\end{cases}
	\]
	which turns \(S\) into a semi-Boolean Heyting semilattice.
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
Given two subobjects \(x \colon X \rightarrowtail H\) and \(y\colon Y \rightarrowtail H\), a \textbf{cooperator} \(\varphi\) on the pair \((X,Y)\) with respect to \(H\) is a morphism \(\varphi \colon X\times Y \rightarrow H\) such that the following diagram commutes.
	\begin{center}
		\begin{tikzcd}[row sep = large]
			X \arrow[r, "{(1_X,0)}"] \arrow[rd, "x"', tail] & X \times Y \arrow[d, "\varphi" description] & Y \arrow[l, "{(0,1_Y)}"'] \arrow[ld, "y", tail] \\
			& H
		\end{tikzcd}
	\end{center}
	When such a cooperator exists, we say that \(X\) and \(Y\) \textbf{cooperate} or \textbf{Huq-commute} in \(H\).
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{proposition commute in hslat}
	Let \(X\), \(Y \subseteq H\) be two subobjects of a Heyting semilattice~\(H\). The following conditions are equivalent:
	\begin{tfae}
		\item \(X\) and \(Y\) Huq-commute in \(H\);
		\item for all \(x \in X\) and \(y \in Y\),
		\begin{align*}
			(x \shortrightarrow y) = y \qquad \text{and} \qquad (y \shortrightarrow x) = x;
		\end{align*}
		\item for all \(x \in X\) and \(y \in Y\), \(x \curlyvee y = 1\).\hfill \qed
	\end{tfae}
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
The \textbf{Huq-commutator} \([X,Y]^{\operatorname{Huq}}\) of \(X\) and \(Y\) in \(H\) is the smallest normal subobject \(N\) of \(H\) such that \(X\) and~\(Y\) cooperate in \({H}/{N}\).
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
Given two subobjects \(X\) and \(Y\) in \(H\), they admit a cooperator if and only if \([X,Y]^{\operatorname{Huq}}=0\).\qed
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\label{definition higgins commutator}
	Let \(x\colon X\rightarrowtail H\) and \(y\colon Y\rightarrowtail H\) be subobjects.
	They induce a morphism \(\langle x,y\rangle\colon X+Y\to H\).
	The \textbf{Higgins commutator} \([X,Y]\) of \(X\) and \(Y\) in~\(H\) is defined as the regular image of \(X\diamond Y\) under \(\langle x,y\rangle\).

	\begin{center}
		\begin{tikzcd}[column sep = large]
			0 \arrow[r]
			& X\diamond Y \arrow[r, Triangle[open, reversed]->] \arrow[d, -Triangle[open], dotted]
			& X+Y \arrow[r, "\Sigma_{X,Y}"] \arrow[d, "{\langle x, y\rangle}"]
			& X\times Y \\
			& {[X,Y]} \arrow[r, tail, dotted]
			& H
		\end{tikzcd}
	\end{center}
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{proposition commutator is intersection}
	Let \(X\), \(Y \subseteq H\) be two subobjects of an (equationally linear) Heyting semilattice \(H\).
	Then the Higgins commutator of \(X\) and \(Y\) in \(H\) is given by
	\[
		[X,Y] = X^{Y} \cap Y^{X},
	\]
	where \(X^{Y}\) denotes the normal closure of \(X\) inside \(X \cup Y\) (and similarly for \(Y^{X}\)).\hfill \qed
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{Remark Split Extension}
	In accordance with Theorem~\ref{BouJa Charact}, for any split extension of Heyting semilattices as in~\eqref{eq:split_ext}, every element \(a \in A\) can be written as
	\[
		a
		= \bigl( (a \shortrightarrow \beta\alpha(a)) \shortrightarrow \beta\alpha(a) \bigr)
		\wedge
		\bigl( ((a \shortrightarrow \beta\alpha(a)) \shortrightarrow \beta\alpha(a)) \shortrightarrow a \bigr),
	\]
	where both
	\(
	a \shortrightarrow \beta\alpha(a)
	\)
	and
	\(
	((a \shortrightarrow \beta\alpha(a)) \shortrightarrow \beta\alpha(a)) \shortrightarrow a
	\)
	belong to \(X\), while \(\beta\alpha(a)\) is in \(B\).
	Equivalently, we may write \(a = (x_1 \shortrightarrow b) \wedge x_2\) for some \(x_1\), \(x_2 \in X\) and \(b \in B\).
	Viewing \(X\) and \(B\) as subobjects of \(A\), we thus see that \(A\) is generated by \(X\) and \(B\).
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
\label{Def Centraliser}
	Let \(X\subseteq H\) be a subobject of an object \(H\). The \textbf{centraliser} \(Z_H(X)\) of \(X\) in \(H\) is the largest subobject of \(H\) which cooperates with \(X\).
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- example-3: body_md -->
In \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{HSLat}}\), the centraliser of \(X\) in \(H\) is given by
	\[
		Z_H(X)
		= \{h\in H \mid \text{for each \(x\in X\), \((x\shortrightarrow h)=h\) and \((h\shortrightarrow x)=x\)}\}\, .
	\]
<!-- end example-3 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{Proposition Centralisers}
	The category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{HSLat}}\) is algebraically cartesian closed. Moreover, centralisers of normal subobjects are normal in~\(\ensuremath{\mathsf{HSLat}}\). \hfill \qed
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{proposition centraliser}
	Let \(H\) be an object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{ELHSLat}}\), and let \(X \subseteq H\) be a subobject. Then the centraliser \(Z_H(X)\) of \(X\) in \(H\) is a normal subobject.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
To show that \(Z_H(X)\) is normal, it suffices to prove that it is a filter in \(H\). Let \(h'\in H\) be such that \(h' \geqslant h\) for some \(h\in Z_H(X)\). Recall (see Proposition~\ref{proposition commute in hslat}) that \(h\in Z_H(X)\) is equivalent to the condition that
	\[
		h \vee x = 1 \quad \text{for all \(x\in X\).}
	\]
	Now, applying the third item of Proposition~\ref{proposition equivalences semi-boolean}, we have
	\[
		1 = h \vee x \;\leqslant\; h' \vee x .
	\]
	Thus \(h'\vee x = 1\) for all \(x\in X\), which implies \(h' \in Z_H(X)\). Hence \(Z_H(X)\) is up-closed, and therefore normal.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{proposition elhslat huq}
	Let \(H\) be an object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{ELHSLat}}\), and let \(X\), \(Y \subseteq H\) be two subobjects. Then, the subobjects \(X\) and \(Y\) Huq-commute in \(H\) if and only if their normal closures \(\bar X\) and \(\bar Y\) have trivial intersection.
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Suppose that \(X\) and \(Y\) Huq-commute. Then, by definition of a centraliser, we have that \(Y \subseteq Z_H(X)\). Since \(Z_H(X)\) is normal in \(H\) by Proposition~\ref{proposition centraliser}, it follows that \(\bar Y \subseteq Z_H(X)\), and hence \(X\) and \(\bar Y\) Huq-commute.
	Applying the same argument again, we obtain \(\bar X \subseteq Z_H(\bar Y)\), so that \(\bar X\) and \(\bar Y\) Huq-commute.

	We conclude using the fact that two subobjects Huq-commute if and only if their Higgins commutator vanishes, together with Proposition~\ref{proposition commutator is intersection}.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
Let \(S\) be a non-empty subset of an equationally linear Heyting semilattice \(H\), and suppose that \(S\) is closed under meets.
	Then the normal subobject \( \bar S \) generated by \(S\) in \(H\) is
	\[
		\bar S \;=\; \{\, s \vee h \mid s \in S,\ h \in H \,\}.
	\]
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
We first prove that \(\bar S\) is a filter of \(H\).
	Let \(h' \in H\) be such that \(h' \ge s \vee h\) for some \(s\in S\) and \(h\in H\).
	Then \(h' = s \vee (h \vee h')\), so \(h'\in \bar S\).
	To show that \(\bar S\) is closed under meets, take \(s,s'\in S\) and \(h,h'\in H\); then
	\begin{align*}
		(s\vee h) \wedge (s'\vee h')
		 & = (s\wedge(s'\vee h')) \vee (h \wedge (s'\vee h'))                               \\
		 & = (s\wedge s') \vee (s\wedge h') \vee (h\wedge s') \vee (h\wedge h') \in \bar S,
	\end{align*}
	where we used that \(S\) is closed under meets and the distribution of the meet over the join given by Proposition~\ref{proposition equivalences semi-boolean}.

	Now let us show that \(\bar S\) is the smallest normal subobject of \(H\) containing \(S\).
	Let \(K \trianglelefteq H\) with \(S \subseteq K\).
	For any \(s\in S\) and \(h\in H\), we have \(s \le s\vee h\); since \(K\) is a filter and contains \(s\), it must also contain \(s\vee h\).
	Thus \(\bar S \subseteq K\), which concludes the proof.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{theorem w}
	Let \(\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}\) be a semi-abelian category. The following conditions are equivalent:
	\begin{tfae}
		\item \(\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}\) satisfies~{\rm (SH)}{} (see~\cite{MFVdL}), and for all subobjects \(X\), \(Y \subseteq A\),
		\[
			\text{\([X,Y] = 0\) \quad if and only if \quad \([\bar X, \bar Y] = 0\);}
		\]
		\item \(\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}\) satisfies~{\rm (W)}{}.\hfill \qed
	\end{tfae}
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{theorem arithmetical and w}
	Let \(\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}\) be a semi-abelian category. The following conditions are equivalent:
	\begin{tfae}
		\item for all subobjects \(X\), \(Y \subseteq A\),
		\[
			[X,Y] = 0 \quad \text{if and only if} \quad \bar X \cap \bar Y = 0;
		\]
		\item \(\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}\) is arithmetical and satisfies condition~{\rm (W)}{}.
	\end{tfae}
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
First observe that, taking \(X = Y = A\), one sees that \(A\) cooperates with itself if and only if \(A\) is the zero object. By Theorem~3.2 of~\cite{HSLat}, this implies that \(\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}\) is arithmetical. Since any arithmetical category satisfies~{\rm (SH)}{}~\cite{MFVdL3}, Theorem~\ref{theorem w} reduces us to showing that for all subobjects \(X\), \(Y \subseteq A\),
	\[
		\text{\([X,Y] = 0\) \quad if and only if \(\quad [\bar X, \bar Y] = 0\).}
	\]
	But when \(\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}\) is arithmetical, we have \([\bar X,\bar Y] = \bar X \cap \bar Y\) by Theorem~3.7 of~\cite{HSLat}, which yields the claim.

	The converse direction follows similarly from Theorem~3.7 of~\cite{HSLat}.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
The category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{ELHSLat}}\) satisfies the condition {\rm (W)}{}.\hfill \qed
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
Let \(H\) be an object of \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{ELHSLat}}\), and let \(X\), \(Y \subseteq H\) be two subobjects. The Huq-commutator of \(X\) and \(Y\) is given by
	\[
		[X,Y]^{\operatorname{Huq}} = \bigl\lbrace (x \vee y) \vee h \;\big|\; x \in X,\, y \in Y,\, h \in H \bigr\rbrace.
	\]
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
By definition, together with Proposition~\ref{proposition commute in hslat}, the Huq-commutator must be the smallest normal subobject of \(H\) containing all elements of the form \(x \vee y\) with \(x \in X\) and \(y \in Y\).

	First, observe that it is indeed a filter. It is clearly up-closed: if \(h' \in H\) satisfies \(h' \geqslant (x \vee y) \vee h\) for some \(x \in X\), \(y \in Y\) and \(h \in H\), then
	\[
		h' = (x \vee y) \vee (h \vee h'),
	\]
	so \(h' \in [X,Y]^{\operatorname{Huq}}\).

	To see that it is closed under meets, take any \(x\), \(x' \in X\), \(y\), \(y' \in Y\) and \(h\), \(h' \in H\). Using the distributivity from Proposition~\ref{proposition equivalences semi-boolean}, we compute:
	\begin{align*}
		(x \vee y \vee h) \wedge (x' \vee y' \vee h') =
		 & \;(x \wedge x') \vee (x \wedge y') \vee (x \wedge h') \vee (y \wedge x') \vee (y \wedge y') \\ & \vee (y \wedge h')
		\vee (h \wedge x') \vee (h \wedge y') \vee (h \wedge h').
	\end{align*}
	This element is clearly greater or equal to \((x \wedge x') \vee (y \wedge y')\), which itself belongs to \([X,Y]^{\operatorname{Huq}}\). Since \([X,Y]^{\operatorname{Huq}}\) is up-closed, the whole meet lies in \([X,Y]^{\operatorname{Huq}}\).

	Finally, suppose that \(K\) is a normal subobject of \(H\) containing every \(x \vee y\) with \(x \in X\) and \(y \in Y\). Then for any \(h \in H\),
	\[
		(x \vee y) \vee h \ge x \vee y,
	\]
	and since \(K\) is up-closed, we have \((x \vee y) \vee h \in K\). Hence \(K\) contains \([X,Y]^{\operatorname{Huq}}\).
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{theorem equivalences ac}
	Let \(\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}\) be a semi-abelian category. The following are equivalent:
	\begin{tfae}
		\item \(\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}\) is algebraically coherent;
		\item for any object \(B\in \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}\), the kernel functor \(\operatorname{Ker}_B \colon \ensuremath{\mathsf{Pt}}_B(\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}) \rightarrow \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}\) preserves binary joins;
		\item for any cospan of sub-split-extensions of the form
		\begin{center}
			\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large,row sep=large]
				X_1 \arrow[r,"\kappa_1"] \arrow[d,"u_1",',tail]
				& A_1 \arrow[r,shift left,"\alpha_1"] \arrow[d,"v_1",',tail]
				& B \arrow[l,shift left,"\beta_1"] \arrow[d,equal] \\
				X \arrow[r,"\kappa"]
				& A \arrow[r,shift left,"\alpha"]
				& B \arrow[l,shift left,"\beta"] \\
				X_2 \arrow[r,"\kappa_2"'] \arrow[u,"u_2",tail]
				& A_2 \arrow[r,shift left,"\alpha_2"] \arrow[u,"v_2",tail]
				& B \arrow[l,shift left,"\beta_2"] \arrow[u,equal]
			\end{tikzcd}
		\end{center}
		with \(A=A_1\cup A_2\), we have that \((X\cap A_1)\cup (X\cap A_2) =X\).\hfill \qed
	\end{tfae}
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{Equations}
	The following identities hold for any equationally linear Heyting semilattice:
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item \(b\lhd(x\shortrightarrow y) = (b\lhd x) \shortrightarrow (b\lhd y)\),
		\item \(b\lhd(x\wedge y) = (b\lhd x) \wedge (b \lhd y)\),
		\item \(b\shortrightarrow x = (b\vee x) \shortrightarrow (b\lhd x)\),
		\item \((x\shortrightarrow b) \shortrightarrow b = ((b \lhd  x) \shortrightarrow (b \vee x))\shortrightarrow (b \vee x)\),
		\item \(b\vee (x\shortrightarrow y) = (((b\lhd x) \shortrightarrow (b\lhd y)) \shortrightarrow (b \vee x)) \shortrightarrow (((b\lhd y) \shortrightarrow (b\lhd x))\shortrightarrow (b \vee y))\),
		\item \((x\shortrightarrow b) \shortrightarrow y = (((b \lhd  x) \shortrightarrow (b \vee y))\shortrightarrow (b \vee y)) \wedge ((b \vee y) \shortrightarrow (b\lhd y))\).
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lemma: useful terms}
	For each \(x \in X_1 \cup X_2\), the elements \(b \lhd x\) and \(x \vee b\) belong to \(X_1 \cup X_2\).
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Let
	\[
		\tilde X \coloneq \{x \in X_1 \cup X_2 \mid \text{\(b \lhd x\) and \(b \vee x\) belong to \(X_1 \cup X_2\)}\}.
	\]
	Noting that each \(X_i\) is contained in \(\tilde X\), it is sufficient to show that \(\tilde X\) is a subalgebra of \(X_1 \cup X_2\) since this would imply that \(\tilde X=X_1\cup X_2\).
	Suppose that \(x\), \(y \in \tilde X\). By Lemma~\ref{Equations}, we have
	\begin{align*}
		b\lhd (x\shortrightarrow y) & = (b\lhd x) \shortrightarrow (b\lhd y),                         \\
		b\lhd (x\wedge y)    & = (b\lhd x) \wedge (b\lhd y),                            \\
		b\vee (x\shortrightarrow y) & = (((b\lhd x) \shortrightarrow (b\lhd y)) \shortrightarrow (b \vee x))
		\shortrightarrow (((b\lhd y) \shortrightarrow (b\lhd x)) \shortrightarrow (b \vee y)),               \\
		b\vee (x\wedge y)    & = (b \vee x) \wedge (b \vee y).
	\end{align*}
	Hence \(\tilde X\) is closed under \(\wedge\) and \(\shortrightarrow\). Since \(1 \in \tilde X\) trivially, this concludes the proof.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lemma: (x-> b)->b and b->x}
	For each \(x \in X_1 \cup X_2\), the elements \((x\shortrightarrow b)\shortrightarrow b\) and \(b\shortrightarrow x\) belong to \(X_1 \cup X_2\).
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
By equations~(3) and~(4) of Lemma~\ref{Equations}, we have
	\begin{align*}
		(x\shortrightarrow b) \shortrightarrow b & = ((b \lhd x) \shortrightarrow (b \vee x)) \shortrightarrow (b \vee x), \\
		b\shortrightarrow x               & = (b \vee x) \shortrightarrow (b \lhd x).
	\end{align*}
	The conclusion then follows from Lemma~\ref{lemma: useful terms}.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lemma: (x->b)->y}
	For each \(x\), \(y \in X_1 \cup X_2\), the element \((x\shortrightarrow b)\shortrightarrow y\) belongs to \(X_1 \cup X_2\).
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
By equation~(6) of Lemma~\ref{Equations}, we have
	\begin{align*}
		(x\shortrightarrow b) \shortrightarrow y
		 & = \bigl((b \lhd x) \shortrightarrow (b \vee y)\bigr)\shortrightarrow (b \vee y)
		\;\wedge\; \bigl((b \vee y) \shortrightarrow (b \lhd y)\bigr).
	\end{align*}
	The conclusion then follows from Lemma~\ref{lemma: useful terms}.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lemma: meet}
	\(\tilde A\) is closed under finite meets.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Suppose that \(a\), \(a' \in \tilde A\). The only case that requires attention is when
	\[
		a = x \wedge (y \shortrightarrow b)
		\quad\text{and}\quad
		a' = x' \wedge (y' \shortrightarrow b).
	\]
	In this case we have
	\[
		a \wedge a' = (x \wedge x') \wedge \bigl((y \vee y')\shortrightarrow b\bigr),
	\]
	which belongs to \(\tilde A\) since \(X_1 \cup X_2\) is closed under \(\wedge\) and \(\vee\).
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
This lemma highlights the importance of \(B\) being the two-element set.
	If \(a' = x' \wedge (y' \shortrightarrow b')\) for some other \(b' \in B\),
	we could not rewrite \(a \wedge a'\) in the desired form.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lemma x -> a and a->x}
	For \(a \in \tilde A\) and \(x \in X_1 \cup X_2\), both \(x \shortrightarrow a\) and \(a \shortrightarrow x\) belong to \(\tilde A\).
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
If \(a \in X_1 \cup X_2\), then \(x \shortrightarrow a\) and \(a \shortrightarrow x\) clearly belong to \(X_1 \cup X_2\).

	Now, suppose that \(a = x' \wedge (x'' \shortrightarrow b)\) for some \(x',x'' \in X_1 \cup X_2\). Then
	\[
		a \shortrightarrow x = x' \shortrightarrow \bigl((x'' \shortrightarrow b)\shortrightarrow x\bigr),
	\]
	which lies in \(X_1 \cup X_2\) by Lemma~\ref{lemma: (x->b)->y}. On the other hand,
	\[
		x \shortrightarrow a = (x \shortrightarrow x') \wedge \bigl((x \wedge x'')\shortrightarrow b\bigr),
	\]
	which belongs to \(\tilde A\) by definition.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lemma: a-->b}
	For any \(a \in \tilde A\), the element \(a \shortrightarrow b\) belongs to \(\tilde A\).
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
If \(a \in X_1 \cup X_2\), then
	\[
		a \shortrightarrow b = 1 \wedge (a \shortrightarrow b),
	\]
	which belongs to \(\tilde A\).
	Suppose now that \(a = x \wedge (y \shortrightarrow b)\) for some \(x\), \(y \in X_1 \cup X_2\).
	Then
	\[
		a \shortrightarrow b = x \shortrightarrow \bigl((y \shortrightarrow b)\shortrightarrow b\bigr),
	\]
	which lies in \(X_1 \cup X_2\) by Lemma~\ref{lemma: (x-> b)->b and b->x}.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lemma: implication}
	\(\tilde A\) is closed under implications.
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Suppose that \(a\), \(a' \in \tilde A\). If \(a' \in X_1 \cup X_2\), then \(a \shortrightarrow a'\) belongs to \(\tilde A\) by Lemma~\ref{lemma x -> a and a->x}. If \(a' = x \wedge (y \shortrightarrow b)\) for some \(x\), \(y\in X_1\cup X_2\), then
	\[
		a \shortrightarrow a' = (a \shortrightarrow x) \wedge \bigl(y \shortrightarrow (a \shortrightarrow b)\bigr).
	\]
	By Lemma~\ref{lemma: a-->b}, the element \(a \shortrightarrow b\) belongs to \(\tilde A\).
	Lemma~\ref{lemma x -> a and a->x} then implies that both
	\(a \shortrightarrow x\) and \(y \shortrightarrow (a \shortrightarrow b)\) lie in \(\tilde A\).
	Finally, Lemma~\ref{lemma: meet} shows that \(a \shortrightarrow a'\) belongs to~\(\tilde A\).
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{theorem: algebraic coherence for 2}
	In the category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{ELHSLat}}\), for any cospan of sub-split-extensions of the form
	\begin{center}
		\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large,row sep=large]
			X_1 \arrow[r,"\kappa_1"] \arrow[d,"u_1",',tail]
			& A_1 \arrow[r,shift left,"\alpha_1"] \arrow[d,"v_1",',tail]
			& B \arrow[l,shift left,"\beta_1"] \arrow[d,equal] \\
			X \arrow[r,"\kappa"]
			& A \arrow[r,shift left,"\alpha"]
			& B \arrow[l,shift left,"\beta"] \\
			X_2 \arrow[r,"\kappa_2"'] \arrow[u,"u_2",tail]
			& A_2 \arrow[r,shift left,"\alpha_2"] \arrow[u,"v_2",tail]
			& B \arrow[l,shift left,"\beta_2"] \arrow[u,equal]
		\end{tikzcd}
	\end{center}
	with \(A=A_1\cup A_2\) and \(B=\{ b,1\}\), we have that \((X\cap A_1)\cup (X\cap A_2) =X\).
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
It remains to prove that \(\tilde A = A\). Indeed, since \(X\) is contained in \(A\), this would imply that for each \(x \in X\) we have either \(x \in X_1 \cup X_2\) or
	\[
		x = x' \wedge (y' \shortrightarrow b)
	\]
	for some \(x',y' \in X_1 \cup X_2\). However, the latter is impossible, since
	\[
		\alpha\bigl(x' \wedge (y' \shortrightarrow b)\bigr) = b,
	\]
	and thus \(x' \wedge (y' \shortrightarrow b)\) cannot lie in the kernel of \(\alpha\). Therefore, we conclude that \(X_1 \cup X_2 = X\).

	Now, applying Remark~\ref{Remark Split Extension}, we know that every element \(a \in A_i\) can be written as
	\[
		a = x \wedge (y \shortrightarrow b')
	\]
	for some \(x\), \(y \in X_i\) and \(b' \in B\). This shows that both \(A_1\) and \(A_2\) are contained in \(\tilde A\). Moreover, \(\tilde A\) trivially contains \(1\), and it follows from Lemma~\ref{lemma: meet} and Lemma~\ref{lemma: implication} that \(\tilde A\) is a subalgebra of \(A\). Hence \(\tilde A = A\), which concludes the proof.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{lemma on coherence}
	In a pointed category \(\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}\) with finite limits, for any split epimorphism
	\(p\colon E \to B\) with kernel \(k\colon N \to E\), if the kernel functor
	\[
		\operatorname{Ker}_B \colon \ensuremath{\mathsf{Pt}}_B(\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}) \to \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}
	\]
	preserves binary joins, then the change-of-base functor
	\[
		k^* \colon \ensuremath{\mathsf{Pt}}_E(\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}) \to \ensuremath{\mathsf{Pt}}_N(\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}})
	\]
	preserves binary joins as well.
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Let \(s\colon B \to E\) be a splitting of \(p\).
	Since pullbacks preserve kernels in pointed categories with finite limits, the diagram
	\[
		\xymatrix{
			\ensuremath{\mathsf{Pt}}_E(\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}) \ar[r]^{k^*} \ar[d]_{Q} &
			\ensuremath{\mathsf{Pt}}_N(\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}) \ar[d]^{P} \\
			\ensuremath{\mathsf{Pt}}_B(\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}) \ar[r]_{\operatorname{Ker}_B} &
			\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}
		}
	\]
	commutes up to isomorphism. Here, \(P\) is the functor sending a point over \(N\) to the domain of its split epimorphism, and \(Q\) sends a point \((C,\gamma,\delta)\) to \((C,p\gamma,\delta s)\).

	Now suppose that \(\operatorname{Ker}_B\) preserves finite joins. Since finite joins in the categories of points are computed as in \(\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}\), we obtain
	\begin{align*}
		P k^*(C_1 \cup C_2)
		 & \cong \operatorname{Ker}_B Q(C_1 \cup C_2)               \\
		 & \cong \operatorname{Ker}_B Q(C_1) \cup \operatorname{Ker}_B Q(C_2)     \\
		 & \cong P k^*(C_1) \cup P k^*(C_2)           \\
		 & \cong P\bigl(k^*(C_1) \cup k^*(C_2)\bigr).
	\end{align*}
	We conclude that
	\[
		k^*(C_1 \cup C_2) \cong k^*(C_1) \cup k^*(C_2),
	\]
	as required.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{proposition ac for finite}
	For each finite equationally linear Heyting semilattice \(B\), the kernel functor
	\[
		\operatorname{Ker}_B \colon \ensuremath{\mathsf{Pt}}_B(\ensuremath{\mathsf{ELHSLat}}) \longrightarrow \ensuremath{\mathsf{ELHSLat}}
	\]
	preserves binary joins.
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
Let \(B\) be a finite equationally linear Heyting semilattice with \(n\) elements.
	The statement is clear for \(n=1\), and the case \(n=2\) was established in
	Proposition~\ref{theorem: algebraic coherence for 2}.
	Assume that the claim holds for any finite equationally linear Heyting semilattice
	with fewer than \(n\) elements.

	Since \(B\) is finite, it is a Heyting algebra, and there exists a unique Heyting
	algebra morphism \(s\colon 2 \to B\), where \(2 \coloneq \{0,1\}\) is the initial object
	in the category of Heyting algebras.
	Viewed as a morphism of Heyting semilattices, \(s\) is a split monomorphism, with
	splitting \(p\colon B \to 2\) given by quotienting by the up-set
	\[
		{\uparrow}{x} \coloneq \{ y \in B \mid y \ge x \}
	\]
	of any minimal element \(x \in B\) amongst elements above the bottom.
	We denote by \(k\colon N \to B\) the kernel of \(p\).

	Since \(N\) has strictly fewer elements than \(B\), the functor \(\operatorname{Ker}_N\) preserves
	binary joins by the induction hypothesis.
	Applying Lemma~\ref{lemma on coherence}, together with the fact that \(\operatorname{Ker}_2\)
	preserves binary joins by Proposition~\ref{theorem: algebraic coherence for 2}, we
	conclude that the change-of-base functor \(k^*\) preserves binary joins.
	Finally, we observe that
	\[
		\operatorname{Ker}_B \cong \operatorname{Ker}_N  k^*,
	\]
	which holds in any pointed category with finite limits. This completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{theorem AC for elhslat}
	The category of equationally linear Heyting semilattices is algebraically coherent.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Consider a cospan of sub-split extensions of the form
	\begin{center}
		\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large,row sep=large]
			X_1 \arrow[r,"\kappa_1"] \arrow[d,"u_1",',tail]
			& A_1 \arrow[r,shift left,"\alpha_1"] \arrow[d,"v_1",',tail]
			& B \arrow[l,shift left,"\beta_1"] \arrow[d,equal] \\
			X \arrow[r,"\kappa"]
			& A \arrow[r,shift left,"\alpha"]
			& B \arrow[l,shift left,"\beta"] \\
			X_2 \arrow[r,"\kappa_2"'] \arrow[u,"u_2",tail]
			& A_2 \arrow[r,shift left,"\alpha_2"] \arrow[u,"v_2",tail]
			& B \arrow[l,shift left,"\beta_2"] \arrow[u,equal]
		\end{tikzcd}
	\end{center}
	with \(A = A_1 \cup A_2\).
	In order to prove algebraic coherence, by Theorem~\ref{theorem equivalences ac}, it suffices to show that
	\[
		X = X_1 \cup X_2,
	\]
	where \(X_1 = X \cap A_1\) and \(X_2 = X \cap A_2\).

	Let \(T\) be the set of all finite subalgebras of \(B\). Clearly,
	\[
		B = \bigcup_{S \in T} S.
	\]
	Recall that in Heyting semilattices every finitely generated algebra is finite (see~\cite{NeWh} or Appendix~\ref{Appendix}).

	By algebraic coherence over finite objects (Proposition~\ref{proposition ac for finite}), for any \(S \in T\) we have
	\begin{align*}
		 & X \cap \bigl((A_1 \cap \alpha^{-1}(S)) \cup (A_2 \cap \alpha^{-1}(S))\bigr)    \\
		 & = (X \cap (A_1 \cap \alpha^{-1}(S))) \cup (X \cap (A_2 \cap \alpha^{-1}(S))) \\
		 & = X_1 \cup X_2 .
	\end{align*}
	Here we used the fact that \(\alpha^{-1}(S)\) contains the kernel of \(\alpha\).
	Since \(\alpha\) is a split epimorphism, it follows that
	\[
		A = \bigcup \{ \alpha^{-1}(S) \mid S \in T \}.
	\]
	Therefore,
	\begin{align*}
		A
		 & = (A_1 \cap A) \cup (A_2 \cap A)                                                                   \\
		 & = \bigcup_{S \in T} (A_1 \cap \alpha^{-1}(S)) \cup \bigcup_{S \in T} (A_2 \cap \alpha^{-1}(S)) \\
		 & = \bigcup_{S \in T} \bigl((A_1 \cap \alpha^{-1}(S)) \cup (A_2 \cap \alpha^{-1}(S))\bigr).
	\end{align*}
	Intersecting with \(X\), we obtain
	\begin{align*}
		X
		 & = \bigcup \{ X \cap ((A_1 \cap \alpha^{-1}(S)) \cup (A_2 \cap \alpha^{-1}(S))) \mid S \in T \} \\
		 & = \bigcup \{ X_1 \cup X_2 \mid S \in T \}                                                            \\
		 & = X_1 \cup X_2,
	\end{align*}
	as required.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
The category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{ELHSLat}}\) satisfies the following properties:
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item change-of-base functors of the fibration of points preserve Higgins and Huq commutators, normal closures, and cokernels;
		\item it satisfies the conditions {\rm (SH)}{} and {\rm (NH)}{};
		\item it is peri-abelian and therefore satisfies the universal central extension condition;
		\item it satisfies {\rm (SSH)}{};
		\item it is strongly protomodular;
		\item it is fibrewise algebraically cartesian closed {\rm (FWACC)}{};
		\item for any normal subobjects \(K,L,M\) of an object \(X\), we have
		      \[
			      [K,L,M] = [[K,L],M] \cup [L,[K,M]]
		      \]
		      as subobjects of \(X\).\hfill \qed
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
Every fibre of the fibration of points in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{ELHSLat}}\) satisfies the condition {\rm (W)}{}.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Let \(S\) and \(T\) be subobjects of an object \(A\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Pt}}_B(\ensuremath{\mathsf{ELHSLat}})\). As explained in~\cite{MFVdL3}, since {\rm (SSH)}{} holds, \(S\) and \(T\) Huq-commute in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Pt}}_B(\ensuremath{\mathsf{ELHSLat}})\) if and only if \(\operatorname{Ker}_B(S)\) and \(\operatorname{Ker}_B(T)\) Huq-commute in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{ELHSLat}}\). By Proposition~\ref{proposition elhslat huq}, this is equivalent to \(\operatorname{Ker}_B(\bar S)\) and \(\operatorname{Ker}_B(\bar T)\) Huq-commuting.	Finally, this holds if and only if \(\bar S\) and \(\bar T\) Huq-commute in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Pt}}_B(\ensuremath{\mathsf{ELHSLat}})\).
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
The category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{ELHSLat}}\) is an algebraic logos.\hfill \qed
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
\label{proposition lacc preserves coproducts}
	If a pointed category \(\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}\) with finite limits is locally algebraically cartesian closed, then for every object \(B\) the kernel functor \(\operatorname{Ker}_B \colon \ensuremath{\mathsf{Pt}}_B(\ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}) \to \ensuremath{\mathcal{C}}\) preserves binary coproducts.
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Under {\rm (LACC)}{} the functor \(\operatorname{Ker}_B \cong (\text{\rm \textexclamdown}_B)^*\) is a left adjoint, hence preserves all colimits, and in particular binary coproducts.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{lemma lacc collapse}
	In \(A_1 +_B A_2\) one has \(x_1 \shortrightarrow x_2 = x_2\).
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Since \(\iota_1\) is a homomorphism, the order relation~\eqref{eq order in A1} gives \(\hat b \leqslant x_1\); as the implication is order-reversing in its first variable, this yields
	\[
		x_1 \shortrightarrow x_2 \leqslant \hat b \shortrightarrow x_2.
	\]
	On the other hand, using \(\iota_1\beta_1 = \iota_2\beta_2\) and the triviality of the action of \(A_2\) from~\eqref{eq trivial action},
	\[
		\hat b \shortrightarrow x_2 = \iota_2(\hat b_2) \shortrightarrow \iota_2\kappa_2(x_2) = \iota_2\bigl(\hat b_2 \shortrightarrow \kappa_2(x_2)\bigr) = \iota_2\kappa_2(x_2) = x_2.
	\]
	Hence \(x_1 \shortrightarrow x_2 \leqslant x_2\). Since \(y \leqslant x \shortrightarrow y\) holds in every Heyting semilattice, we also have \(x_2 \leqslant x_1 \shortrightarrow x_2\), and therefore \(x_1 \shortrightarrow x_2 = x_2\).
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{lemma lacc free}
	In the coproduct \(X_1 + X_2\) of the kernels, taken in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{ELHSLat}}\), one has \(x_1 \shortrightarrow x_2 \neq x_2\).
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
Let \(f \colon X_1 + X_2 \to B = \{b < 1\}\) be the homomorphism determined by the homomorphisms \(X_1 \to B\colon x_1 \mapsto b\) and \(X_2 \to B\colon x_2 \mapsto b\) (each sends the non-top element to \(b\) and is a homomorphism of two-element chains). Then
	\[
		f(x_1 \shortrightarrow x_2) = f(x_1) \shortrightarrow f(x_2) = b \shortrightarrow b = 1, \qquad \text{whereas} \qquad f(x_2) = b.
	\]
	As \(1 \neq b\), the elements \(x_1 \shortrightarrow x_2\) and \(x_2\) of \(X_1 + X_2\) are distinct.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{theorem not lacc}
	The variety \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{ELHSLat}}\) of equationally linear Heyting semilattices is not locally algebraically cartesian closed.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
Consider the comparison morphism
	\[
		c \colon X_1 + X_2 \longrightarrow \operatorname{Ker}_B(A_1 +_B A_2)
	\]
	of~\eqref{eq comparison} attached to the two points \(A_1\) and \(A_2\) constructed above. By definition \(c\) restricts to \(\iota_i\kappa_i\) on \(X_i\), so it is a homomorphism sending the generators \(x_1\), \(x_2\) of \(X_1 + X_2\) to the elements denoted \(x_1\), \(x_2\) in \(A_1 +_B A_2\). Using Lemma~\ref{lemma lacc collapse},
	\[
		c(x_1 \shortrightarrow x_2) = c(x_1) \shortrightarrow c(x_2) = x_1 \shortrightarrow x_2 = x_2 = c(x_2).
	\]
	By Lemma~\ref{lemma lacc free}, however, \(x_1 \shortrightarrow x_2 \neq x_2\) in \(X_1 + X_2\). Therefore \(c\) is not a monomorphism, so it is not an isomorphism, and consequently \(\operatorname{Ker}_B\) does not preserve the binary coproduct \(A_1 +_B A_2\). By Proposition~\ref{proposition lacc preserves coproducts}, \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{ELHSLat}}\) is not locally algebraically cartesian closed.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{theorem not cosmash}
	The category \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{ELHSLat}}\) is not cosmash associative.
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
Let \(X=Y=Z\) be the free equationally linear Heyting semilattice on a single generator, that is, the two-element chain, and write \(x\), \(y\), \(z\) for the respective generators. Then \(X+Y+Z\) is the free equationally linear Heyting semilattice on \(\{x,y,z\}\), which is finite by~\cite{NeWh} (see also Appendix~\ref{Appendix}). Consider the element
	\[
		f \coloneq (x\shortrightarrow y) \shortrightarrow \bigl((z\shortrightarrow x)\shortrightarrow y\bigr).
	\]

	\emph{The element \(f\) belongs to \(X\diamond Y\diamond Z\).} Indeed, sending any single generator to \(1\) reduces \(f\) to \(1\):
	\begin{align*}
		f|_{x=1} & = (1\shortrightarrow y)\shortrightarrow\bigl((z\shortrightarrow 1)\shortrightarrow y\bigr) = y\shortrightarrow(1\shortrightarrow y) = y\shortrightarrow y = 1, \\
		f|_{y=1} & = (x\shortrightarrow 1)\shortrightarrow\bigl((z\shortrightarrow x)\shortrightarrow 1\bigr) = 1\shortrightarrow 1 = 1,                            \\
		f|_{z=1} & = (x\shortrightarrow y)\shortrightarrow\bigl((1\shortrightarrow x)\shortrightarrow y\bigr) = (x\shortrightarrow y)\shortrightarrow(x\shortrightarrow y) = 1,
	\end{align*}
	using the identities \(1\shortrightarrow a = a\) and \(a\shortrightarrow 1 = 1\). Hence \(f\in X\diamond Y\diamond Z\).

	\emph{The element \(f\) does not belong to \(\langle X\diamond Y, Z\rangle\).} We first observe that \(X\diamond Y = \mathord{\uparrow}(x\vee y)\), the principal filter generated by \(x\vee y\) in \(X+Y\). Indeed, since \(X\cup Y = X+Y\), the induced morphism \(\langle x,y\rangle\) is the identity, so the Higgins commutator \([X,Y]\) coincides with the cosmash product \(X\diamond Y\); by Proposition~\ref{proposition commutator is intersection} it equals \(X^{X+Y}\cap Y^{X+Y} = \mathord{\uparrow}x \cap \mathord{\uparrow}y = \mathord{\uparrow}(x\vee y)\).

	Now consider the homomorphism
	\[
		\varphi\colon X+Y+Z \longrightarrow C\times C', \qquad
		\varphi(x) = (0,0),\quad \varphi(y)=(1,2),\quad \varphi(z)=(0,1),
	\]
	into the product of the chains \(C=\{0<1<2\}\) and \(C'=\{0<1<2<3\}\). A direct computation gives
	\[
		\varphi(f) = (1,3) \qquad\text{and}\qquad \varphi(x\vee y) = (1,2).
	\]
	The image of \(X+Y\) under \(\varphi\) is the subalgebra generated by \((0,0)\) and \((1,2)\), namely the chain \(\{(0,0),(1,2),(2,3)\}\). Hence for every \(w\in X\diamond Y\) we have \(\varphi(w)\in\{(0,0),(1,2),(2,3)\}\) and, since \(w\geqslant x\vee y\) and \(\varphi\) preserves the order, also \(\varphi(w)\geqslant(1,2)\); therefore \(\varphi(w)\in\{(1,2),(2,3)\}\). Together with \(\varphi(z)=(0,1)\), this shows that \(\varphi\) maps \(\langle X\diamond Y, Z\rangle\) into the three-element chain
	\[
		D = \{(0,1),\,(1,2),\,(2,3)\},
	\]
	which is a subalgebra of \(C\times C'\) (its top \((2,3)\) being that of the whole product). As \(\varphi(f)=(1,3)\notin D\), we conclude that \(f\notin\langle X\diamond Y, Z\rangle\).

	By the discussion preceding the theorem, the comparison \(c\colon (X\diamond Y)\diamond Z\to X\diamond Y\diamond Z\) is not surjective, hence not an isomorphism. Therefore \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{ELHSLat}}\) is not cosmash associative.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
